title: The forty who came back
hookLine: tradition says forty who had deserted returned with Mai Bhago and died at Khidrana; the Guru tore up their letter of leaving
last: SAHIBZADE — THE YOUNGEST WERE THE BRAVEST.

lines: FORTY SIGN A PAPER AND LEAVE.
cards: I'm out. Don't call me. Leaving the group.

A message like that feels final the moment it's sent. Go back to Anandpur, months under siege, food gone, no end in sight. A band of Sikhs from the Majha country near Amritsar can't take any more and want to go home.
Tradition says the Guru told them: if you go, write it down. Say you are no longer my Sikhs. Forty of them signed the paper and walked out.
At home, nobody welcomed them. And one woman from their own country, Mai Bhago, would not let them rest.

teach.b: Chali Mukte. Chali means forty; mukte, the liberated ones, the freed. It's a strange name for men who deserted, and that's the point.

teach.h: MAI BHAGO RIDES, AND THEY FOLLOW.
teach.b: Tradition says Mai Bhago shamed them: if they wouldn't stand with the Guru, she would go herself. She rode out, and the forty rode with her.
By then the Guru was on the run through the dry country after Chamkaur, with a Mughal force behind him.

They caught up near a pool called Khidrana, around the end of 1705 by the usual dating, and the forty and Mai Bhago stood between the Guru and his pursuers. When the fierce fighting was over, all forty had fallen.
Mai Bhago was wounded, and lived. Then the story slows down.

teach.h: THE GURU TEARS UP THE PAPER.
teach.b: The Guru walked the field, the story goes, from man to man, lifting each head, wiping each face, calling each by name. One of them, Mahan Singh, was still breathing. The Guru asked what he wanted.
Not a reward. Just this: tear up the paper. The Guru had kept it all this time.
He took it out and tore it up. The place was renamed Muktsar, the pool of liberation, and Sikhs still gather there every year. The story doesn't pretend they never left.
The paper was real; they signed it. And still the Guru tore it up.
Every day, in the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh worship, the forty are remembered together under that name: not as deserters, but as the ones who came back.

how: Sikhs remember the Chali Mukte, the forty liberated ones, in the Ardas said at the close of worship every day, and each year a gathering at Muktsar in Punjab marks the battle of Khidrana.

o: forty men freed from a Mughal prison
the forty who left the Guru and came back
forty saints who never left the Guru's side

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

the Guru had kept the paper they signed

they did leave, and signed a paper saying so. the story doesn't hide it; it ends with the paper torn up.

games.q: you're the Guru, walking the field. the last of the forty who once signed away their bond with you is dying, and he asks for one thing. what do you do?
o: keep the paper, as a record of what happened.
take it out and tear it up.
games.why: tradition says the Guru had kept the paper all along, and tore it up in front of Mahan Singh. the place became Muktsar, the pool of liberation.

practice: Think of someone who walked away from you, or someone you walked away from: a friend who drifted, a cousin after an argument, maybe a practice or a promise you left behind.
Picture the paper, whatever it was, the last text, the slammed door, and see it torn in two; you don't have to fix anything, just let there be a door. If you pray, you can hold them in that prayer.

wordCard.voice: Chali Mukte. The forty liberated ones, who left and came back. Your week: Panj Pyare, amrit, Khalsa, the river, Chamkaur, the Sahibzade, and now the forty.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the forty liberated ones.

carryVoice: Your line: you can always come back. A torn paper, a door held open. See you tomorrow.
